scn_pwr_tutorial_brief: Guided practice without leaderboard scoring. You take over a hot, subcritical PWR: the shutdown bank and boron concentration are prepared, the control bank is inserted, pumps are stopped and the turbine valve is closed. This is not a thermal cold start. Inspect the starting state, establish circulation, carefully raise power, then take on 150 MWe of grid load. The tutorial card shows your task, current readings and contextual hints. Objectives count only when plant conditions are met; elapsed time alone is not enough. A low core flow alarm is expected initially while pumps are stopped. Leave pressurizer and feedwater control in automatic. Pause to read and initially use 1× for rod movement; cautiously speed up a slow power rise. Completion requires 120 consecutive stable simulation seconds. An unfinished attempt ends without success after 60 simulation minutes. You can restart after a scram or plant loss.
tut_unranked: Practice without points or leaderboard entry. Review your completed objectives and shift history.
tut_timeout: Practice time expired: some learning objectives are still pending.
tut_hold: Conditions met: {held}/{required} consecutive simulation seconds. This hold time resets if conditions are lost.
tut_inspect_instruction: Check pressure and temperature in the primary panel and negative reactivity in the core panel. Expected: 140–164 bar, 270–305 °C average temperature and neutron power below 0.1%. Read the diagnostics for the stopped pumps.
tut_inspect_why: Subcritical means a self-sustaining chain reaction has not yet been established. Hot coolant does not by itself mean the reactor is producing power. The starting conditions are checked for five seconds; a click cannot confirm them.
tut_inspect_values: Pressure {pressure} bar · Average temperature {temperature} °C · Reactivity {rho} pcm
tut_pumps_instruction: Switch on all four pumps in the primary panel. Use diagnostics to check that their actual speeds reach at least 90%. Target: at least 18,000 kg/s core flow for three seconds.
tut_pumps_why: A drive command does not immediately produce full flow. Sufficient actual circulation is needed to carry heat away from the core.
tut_pumps_values: Pumps at 90% or more: {pumps}/4 · Core flow {flow} kg/s · Pressure {pressure} bar
tut_power_instruction: In the core panel, use short Withdraw pulses and wait for actual rod movement. Aim for roughly +50 to +100 pcm reactivity. If reactivity is higher, carefully Insert; do not hold Withdraw continuously. Target: neutron power of at least 2% with circulation maintained. Leave turbine control in manual at 0% for now.
tut_power_why: Positive reactivity makes power rise with a delay. Further rod movement during that delay can accelerate the rise unnecessarily. Watch reactivity and reactor period alongside neutron power. The prepared boron concentration does not need changing for this startup path.
tut_power_values: Neutron power {neutron}% · Reactivity {rho} pcm · Core flow {flow} kg/s
tut_load_title: Coordinate heat removal and load pickup
tut_load_instruction: The exercise now requests 150 MWe. Switch rod control in the core panel and turbine control in the secondary panel to automatic; keep feedwater in automatic too. Watch valve opening, steam and feedwater flow. Target: 140–160 MWe, 10–20% thermal power, 35–65% steam generator level and 140–164 bar primary pressure for 15 seconds.
tut_load_why: The turbine valve admits steam to produce electrical power. Feedwater replaces the mass removed, while rod control adjusts average temperature to the requested load. Compare commands and responses in diagnostics.
tut_load_values: Electrical {electric} MWe · Thermal power {power}% · Level {level}% · Pressure {pressure} bar
tut_stable_instruction: Hold the previous step’s conditions for 120 uninterrupted seconds. Reactivity must also stay between −30 and +30 pcm; a positive power rise must not have a period below 60 seconds. Watch trends and avoid unnecessary adjustments.
tut_stable_why: A brief in-range reading does not establish stable operation. The shared hold time checks whether power delivery, heat removal and water inventory remain in balance. Leaving the required range resets only the current hold time.
tut_stable_values: Electrical {electric} MWe · Thermal power {power}% · Level {level}% · Reactivity {rho} pcm
tut_hint_pressure: Pressure is outside the learning target. Check pressurizer control and set it to automatic. Pay attention to active trip alarms.
tut_hint_pumps: Switch on each of the four pumps in the primary panel. Then wait for spin-up; a green drive state alone is not enough.
tut_hint_inspect: Pause to read if needed. The simulation must run for the condition check. The tiny initial neutron signal does not mean load has been picked up.
tut_hint_fast: The rise is too strong. Return to 1×, release Withdraw and reduce reactivity with short Insert pulses. If trip alarms occur, scram is the way to stop this attempt.
tut_hint_travel: The rods are still moving to the requested position. Wait for actual position to catch up before issuing another pulse.
tut_hint_pull: Reactivity is still below +50 pcm. Give a short Withdraw pulse and observe the response instead of stacking commands.
tut_hint_insert: Reactivity is above +100 pcm. Carefully reduce it with short Insert pulses and wait for the actual rod position.
tut_hint_wait: Reactivity is in the intended startup band. Wait for power to rise. Cautious time acceleration can shorten the wait; return to 1× before further rod movements.
tut_hint_auto: For load pickup, rod, turbine and feedwater control must be in automatic. The exercise supplies the 150 MWe demand.
tut_hint_level: Steam generator level is outside 35–65%. Check automatic feedwater control and compare steam and feedwater flow.
tut_hint_settle: Allow the controllers to settle and watch the hold timer. If it returns to zero, at least one target condition was lost.
diag_frozen: Measurement unavailable: gauge holds the last value, not the current level.
diag_flow_note: Pumps can coast down after switching OFF. Core flow includes natural circulation. Interlocks may limit valve requests; opening alone does not guarantee flow.
learn_note: Operator actions are requests, not confirmation of their effect. Cleared alarms indicate recovery of the corresponding limit. A preceding action may have helped; timing alone does not prove causation.
learn_empty: No faults, alarm transitions or operator actions were recorded for this section. Older saves do not contain this history.
learn_truncated: History is incomplete: up to 600 entries are shown.
learn_first: First recorded warning or trip signal: {time} · {alarm}
start_intro: You are the reactor operator. Keep the plant inside its envelope, follow grid demand and master the faults.
opt_cold_start: Hot subcritical start (bring it up yourself) -- free play only
reactor_pwr_desc: Two separate loops, 158 bar, no boiling in the core. Power is set with control rods and boric acid. Every feedback is negative — forgiving, but slow to respond.
reactor_bwr_desc: A single loop, steam goes straight to the turbine. Recirculation flow moves power within seconds. At low flow and high power the density-wave instability is waiting.
reactor_rbmk_desc: Historical graphite-moderated pressure-tube reactor before the retrofits. Positive void feedback and a geometric graphite displacer effect. Watch the shutdown margin.
alarm_help_none: No further explanation on file — the entry already speaks for itself.
stats_cfg_hint: Choose which values appear in the header bar -- separately per reactor type, saved for you. Applies immediately. You can also reorder them right there by dragging (press and hold, then move).
glossary_intro: The key terms in short — not a course, just a reference.
shortcuts_intro: Work anywhere during a running game, except while typing in a text field.
sc_escape_d: Close the active help window (alarm help, panel window, briefing)
sc_menu_d: Back to the main menu (asks first)
sc_scram_d: Hold for one second to trigger the scram
sc_panel_core_d: Open Reactor core as a window
sc_panel_prim_d: Open Primary loop as a window
sc_panel_sec_d: Open Secondary loop as a window
sc_panel_grid_d: Open Generator and grid as a window
sc_panel_mimic_d: Open Plant mimic as a window
sc_panel_trend_d: Open Trend recorders as a window
sc_panel_chem_d: Open Reactor chemistry as a window
gl_reactivity_d: How far the core sits from a self-sustaining steady chain reaction. Positive means power is rising on its own. pcm (hundred-thousandths) is the physical unit; $ (dollars) measures the same value relative to the delayed-neutron fraction — at 1 $ the chain reaction goes "prompt critical" (see there).
gl_period_d: Time for power to change by a factor of e (≈2.72). Short and positive means trouble is close. Infinite means stable.
gl_prompt_d: Reactivity reaches the delayed-neutron fraction (β, usually 1 $). From here the chain reaction sustains itself on prompt neutrons alone — power no longer rises over seconds, but over milliseconds.
gl_dnbr_d: Margin to the boiling crisis: how much power is left before the coolant film on the fuel cladding dries out completely and cooling breaks down. DNBR on the pressurized-water design, CPR on the two boiling ones — below 1 the limit is crossed.
gl_subcooling_d: Margin of coolant temperature below the saturation temperature at the current pressure. As it falls toward zero, the coolant starts boiling where the design never intended it to.
gl_xenon_d: Xe-135 builds up during operation and absorbs neutrons. After a power cut it keeps building for hours, fed by the decay of its precursor iodine-135 — reactivity keeps falling before it recovers.
gl_samarium_d: Sm-149 acts like xenon but is stable — it doesn't decay away, it has to be burned out by fissioning. After a long shutdown the poisoning just sits there instead of fading.
gl_orm_d: Operating reactivity margin on the RBMK, expressed as equivalent rod worth. The game estimates it from two rod-bank positions and uses it in void feedback; real ORM also depends on spatial neutron flux.
gl_void_d: How reactivity responds to steam voids in the coolant. Negative (pressurized- and boiling-water designs) is self-limiting: more steam means less reactivity. Positive (RBMK at low operating margin) is self-reinforcing.
gl_doppler_d: As fuel temperature rises, the U-238 resonances broaden and absorb more neutrons — always negative, acts instantly, and the fastest built-in brake on all three plant types.
gl_decay_d: Heat from the radioactive decay of fission products, which keeps going even after a scram — starting around 7% of rated power, then fading slowly over hours and days. The reason a shut-down core still needs cooling.
gl_scram_d: Reactor trip: every rod drives in at maximum speed. Named differently by control room — RESA in German, SCRAM in American usage, AZ-5 on the RBMK. Never fires on its own — what a given alarm means is in its own help text on the annunciator.
gl_annun_d: New (fast blink + horn): just came in, unacknowledged. Acknowledged (steady light): seen, cause still present. Cleared (slow blink): cause gone, but not yet acknowledged. Dark: everything normal.
empty_stage: This area is filled in a later version.
fault_body: The simulation reached an invalid state and was stopped. That is a bug in the game, not your mistake.
footer_note: Physically modelled, but a game — not a training simulator.
reactor_soon_hint: This type arrives in a later version. The pressurised water reactor is already playable.
ctl_boron_hint: Takes about three minutes to arrive.
trip_power_high_help:
Neutron flux is above the permitted limit — 112% for the pressurized water reactor and RBMK, and 118% for the boiling water reactor. Without corrective action, reactor power will continue to rise within seconds.

Actions:
1. Initiate an immediate reactor trip — press the button at the upper right of the header twice (SCRAM, or AZ-5 for the RBMK). No other control can reduce reactivity quickly enough.
2. Determine the cause before restarting. Common causes are withdrawing "Control rods" (Reactor Core panel) too quickly or making an excessively large change to "Load demand" (Generator and Grid panel).
3. Before restarting, press "Reset" on the alarm panel. This is only possible once no trip alarm remains active.
trip_period_short_help:
The reactor period is below 10 seconds while the chain reaction is active. Reactor power is increasing too rapidly for normal control systems to compensate sufficiently.

Actions:
1. Initiate an immediate reactor trip (SCRAM/AZ-5, header, press twice).
2. The most common cause is withdrawing "Control rods" (Reactor Core panel) too quickly or introducing unintended positive reactivity — for example "Boric acid → Dilute" (Reactor Chemistry panel) in the pressurized water reactor.
3. During the next startup, move the control rods much more slowly or operate "Rod control" or "Power controller" (Reactor Core panel) in automatic mode.

For reference: a reactor period of 10 s means that power increases by a factor of e every 10 seconds, corresponding to more than twenty times the initial power within one minute.
trip_pzr_press_low_help:
Pressurizer pressure is below 132 bar. Possible causes include a coolant leak — such as a stuck relief valve — or an unfavorable balance between pressurizer spray and heater power.

As pressure decreases, the boiling temperature of the coolant also decreases. The subcooling margin therefore becomes smaller. At zero subcooling margin, the thermal reserve to boiling is lost and heat removal in the primary circuit deteriorates significantly.

Actions:
1. If "Relief valve stuck open" is also present on the alarm panel, first set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary Circuit panel). This stops the coolant loss. As long as the leak remains open, primary pressure cannot be stabilized permanently.
2. Initiate SCRAM.
3. Check "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary Circuit panel). If automatic control is insufficient, switch to manual and increase heater power.
4. Reduce "Pressuriser spray" if it is manually open.

The key indication for this condition is the subcooling margin, not pressurizer pressure alone.
trip_pzr_press_high_help:
Pressurizer pressure is above 166 bar. A common cause is insufficient spray flow while reactor power is increasing. The relief valve opens automatically at 162 bar and the safety valves open at 171 bar.

Actions:
1. Initiate SCRAM.
2. Switch "Pressuriser spray" (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and open it if automatic control does not limit the pressure sufficiently.
3. Reduce "Pressuriser heaters". Do not operate heating and spraying against each other, as this causes additional pressure oscillations.
4. After reset, perform power changes more slowly. Rapid power increases are a common cause of excessive pressurizer pressure.
trip_pzr_level_low_help:
Pressurizer level is below 17%. This does not yet initiate a reactor trip, but it can precede a pressure decrease. The pressurizer provides the steam volume required for primary pressure control; at an excessively low level, stable pressure control can no longer be maintained reliably.

Actions:
- Check for coolant loss. If "PORV open" or "Relief valve stuck open" is present on the alarm panel, set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary Circuit panel).
- Limit power changes until the level stabilizes. Pressurizer level depends on average coolant temperature: as the primary circuit cools, coolant volume decreases and the pressurizer level falls.
- If the level does not recover, monitor for an actual pressure deviation (see "Pressure low").
trip_dnbr_low_help:
DNBR is below 1.3. The safety margin to departure from nucleate boiling at the fuel cladding is nearly exhausted. Below 1.0, the liquid film at the fuel surface can break down and local cladding temperature can rise rapidly.

Three parameters have a major influence on DNBR: high coolant flow increases the margin, while high reactor power and low subcooling reduce it.

Actions:
1. Initiate SCRAM. With power and coolant flow unchanged, DNBR cannot recover sufficiently.
2. Check "Reactor coolant pumps" (Primary Circuit panel). A failed pump can be selected there and restarted.
3. If "Subcooling low" is also active, low primary pressure is the main cause. Follow the actions described for that condition.
4. After reset, restart more slowly and do not increase power until all required pumps are operating.
trip_sg_level_low_help:
Steam generator level is below 25%. Tube bundles may become uncovered and cavitation can occur at the feedwater pumps. The steam generator is the heat sink for the primary circuit; at very low level, heat transfer becomes increasingly restricted.

Actions:
1. Initiate SCRAM.
2. Check "Feedwater" (Secondary Circuit panel). If the level continues to decrease in automatic mode, switch to manual and increase feedwater flow.
3. Common causes are loss of feedwater or excessive steam removal due to "Governor valve" (Secondary Circuit panel) being opened too far.

When reading the level indication, note that after a load rejection the pressure can decrease and the water can swell. The indicated level may therefore rise temporarily even though the actual water inventory is decreasing.
alarm_sg_level_high_help:
Steam generator level is above 78%. Water may be carried with the steam toward the turbine, creating a risk of water hammer.

Actions:
- Reduce "Feedwater" (Secondary Circuit panel). If necessary, briefly switch to manual and lower the level.
- Check whether the high level is only a transient overshoot of the automatic control system following a load change. In this case, the value may stabilize after several seconds. The feedwater controller uses steam flow as a feed-forward signal and requires a short adjustment period following load changes.
alarm_sg_press_high_help:
Steam pressure in the steam generator is above 84 bar. Steam removal through the control valve is lower than the current steam generation rate. At 88 bar, the secondary-side safety valves open.

Actions:
- Check "Governor valve" (Secondary Circuit panel). If automatic control is insufficient, briefly switch to manual and open it further.
- Alternatively, reduce "Load demand" (Generator and Grid panel) until steam pressure stabilizes.
- The steam bypass system opens automatically at 72 bar and routes excess steam directly to the condenser, bypassing the turbine. No manual operation is required; its current contribution is displayed in the Secondary Circuit panel.
trip_rcp_lost_help:
Coolant flow is below 60% of nominal flow. At least one main coolant pump has failed or been switched off, or the remaining total flow is no longer sufficient for the required heat removal.

A second and more critical possibility is steam entering the pump suction. The pumps may continue to run while mass flow decreases sharply. If coolant flashes because of a pressure decrease, its density falls and the actual mass flow drops even though pump speed remains unchanged.

Actions:
1. Initiate SCRAM.
2. Check "Reactor coolant pumps" (Primary Circuit panel). A failed pump can be selected there and restarted.
3. If the subcooling margin is simultaneously at or below zero, pressure loss is the primary problem. First stop any existing leak ("Block valve", Primary Circuit panel) and then restore pressure.
4. Do not increase reactor power again until the trip has been reset and all required pumps are operating.
alarm_subcool_low_help:
The subcooling margin is below 8 K. Coolant temperature is approaching the saturation temperature corresponding to the current pressure.

Subcooling margin is a key primary-circuit parameter. It indicates the temperature difference between the coolant and saturation. At zero subcooling margin, no thermal reserve to boiling remains and heat removal can subsequently deteriorate significantly.

Actions:
1. Determine the cause of the pressure decrease. If "Relief valve stuck open" is active, set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary Circuit panel).
2. Increase pressure: switch "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and increase heater power; close "Pressuriser spray".
3. Alternatively or additionally, reduce reactor power before the DNBR limit is crossed.
4. Check "Reactor coolant pumps". Reduced coolant flow further decreases the safety margin.
alarm_porv_open_help:
The pressurizer relief valve is open and is reducing primary-circuit pressure. It opens as designed at 162 bar and closes automatically once sufficient pressure has been relieved.

If the indication remains active at a substantially lower pressure, the valve may be stuck open. In that case, "Relief valve stuck open" also appears. As long as the valve remains open, the primary circuit continuously loses coolant.

Actions:
- If the indication appears only during a pressure spike and then clears, no direct action on the valve is required. Check "Pressuriser spray" and "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary Circuit panel) to prevent another pressure increase.
- If the indication remains active, set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary Circuit panel). The block valve is installed in series upstream of the relief valve and stops the coolant loss.
- Monitor pressurizer level and subcooling margin. These values provide early indication of continuing coolant loss.
alarm_turbine_trip_help:
Following a turbine trip, the generator is disconnected from the grid and turbine load is removed. Reactor heat must now be transferred to the condenser through the steam bypass system and, if required, additionally relieved through safety valves.

Actions:
1. Stabilize the plant and monitor pressure and water levels. Both parameters can fluctuate significantly following a load rejection.
2. Reconnect to the grid using "Reconnect turbine" (Generator and Grid panel) only after the plant has stabilized. Turbine connection is only possible once no reactor trip remains active.
3. Then increase "Load demand" (same panel) gradually.

If the turbine trip occurred together with a reactor trip, reset the alarm panel first.
trip_clad_temp_help:
Cladding temperature is above 1204 °C. In this temperature range, the zirconium-water reaction generates additional heat and hydrogen. If the temperature remains above this value for more than three minutes, core loss occurs — even without a preceding power excursion, solely because of inadequate cooling.

Actions:
1. Initiate an immediate reactor trip (SCRAM/AZ-5) if this has not already occurred.
2. Restore heat removal. The available method depends on the current plant condition:
   - "Reactor coolant pumps" or "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel) if electrical power and sufficient water are available.
   - "Isolation condenser" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems section) if main steam is isolated.
   - "Diesel fire-water pump (below 12 bar)" (same section) if no electrical power remains. This system requires no motor or electronics.
3. Check primary pressure and subcooling. If subcooling margin is below zero, increasing pump speed alone is insufficient. The required pressure must first be restored.
event_h2_explosion: Hydrogen explosion in the reactor building
event_time_skip: Time skipped ahead until the xenon had decayed
trip_dome_press_high_help:
Dome or drum pressure is above the permitted value — 78.5 bar for the boiling water reactor and 76 bar for the RBMK. Steam generation is greater than the amount of steam being removed.

This condition is particularly critical in the boiling water reactor. As pressure rises, the steam void fraction in the core decreases. Moderation therefore increases, adding positive reactivity. A positive feedback between rising pressure and increasing reactor power can develop.

First determine why steam removal is restricted.

Is "MSIV closed" or "Main steam isolation stuck" also active?

If so, the control valve and steam bypass system are ineffective because both are located downstream of the closed isolation valves.

1. Initiate SCRAM (header, press twice).
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems section). Under these conditions it provides the available heat sink and is effective only after the reactor has been shut down. Therefore complete step 1 first.
3. Monitor containment pressure and vent in time.

No main-steam isolation alarm present?

The normal steam path is then available:
- Switch "Governor valve" (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and open it further.
- The steam bypass system opens automatically at 4 bar above operating pressure.
- In the boiling water reactor, reduce "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel). This directly reduces reactor power without moving a control rod.

At 78 bar, the safety valves open and discharge steam into the suppression chamber. This limits reactor pressure but simultaneously increases containment loading.
trip_level_low_help:
Water level is below 25%. Adequate core coverage is at risk. If fuel elements become uncovered, heat transfer deteriorates significantly.

Actions:
1. Initiate SCRAM/AZ-5.
2. Check "Feedwater" (Secondary Circuit panel). If automatic control is insufficient, switch to manual and increase feedwater flow.
3. If AC power is unavailable, the feedwater pumps and their control system are unavailable. "Diesel fire-water pump (below 12 bar)" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems section) then remains available. It requires no motor or electronics but provides a much lower flow rate.
4. Do not increase reactor power again until water level is stable within the normal range.

The level indication requires DC power. If DC power is lost, the displayed value may remain frozen at the last measurement while the actual water level continues to fall. This behavior also played an important role during the Fukushima accident in 2011.
alarm_level_high_help:
Water level is above 78%. Water may be carried with the steam toward the turbine.

Actions:
- Reduce "Feedwater" (Secondary Circuit panel); if required, switch to manual and reduce flow.
- Check whether the elevated level is only a transient control-system overshoot following a load change. In that case, the value may stabilize without further action.
- If the level continues to rise despite reduced feedwater flow, steam removal is lower than steam generation. Check the main steam path (see "Dome pressure high").
trip_oprm_help:
A power oscillation has been detected and the OPRM limit has been exceeded. The operating point is in the restricted region of the power-flow map: high reactor power combined with insufficient recirculation flow.

In this region, steam void fraction, pressure loss and coolant flow couple into a density-wave oscillation. Its amplitude increases instead of decaying and can eventually result in fuel-cladding damage.

Actions:
1. Initiate SCRAM. With an active OPRM alarm, this is the safe response because the oscillation amplitude increases faster than the operating point can be shifted sufficiently.
2. The cause is "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel) being too low for the current reactor power.
3. For future operation: increase coolant flow first and then increase power using the control rods. Reversing this sequence can move the operating point through the restricted region of the map.
alarm_instability_help:
There are indications of a power oscillation. The decay ratio is approaching 1. At a value of 1, a disturbance no longer decays; above 1, its amplitude increases. The OPRM limit has not yet been reached, so the condition can still be corrected without a reactor trip.

Actions:
1. Increase "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel). Higher flow reduces the steam void fraction and directly damps the density-wave oscillation.
2. If this is insufficient, reduce reactor power until the operating point has left the restricted region of the map: "Control rods → Insert" (Reactor Core panel).

Without corrective action, the oscillation amplitude can continue to increase until the OPRM threshold is reached. A reactor trip is then required.
alarm_recirc_low_help:
Recirculation flow is too low for the current high reactor power. The operating point is at the edge of the instability region and therefore close to conditions in which density-wave oscillations can occur.

Actions:
1. Increase "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel) BEFORE reactor power rises further.
2. If sufficient flow cannot be established, reduce reactor power instead of maintaining it by withdrawing additional control rods.

Rule for this reactor type: increase flow first, then power. Reversing the sequence can move the operating point through the restricted region of the power-flow map.
alarm_msiv_closed_help:
The main steam isolation valves are closed. The steam path to the turbine and condenser is interrupted. The normal heat-removal path is therefore unavailable and reactor pressure rises.

Important: "Governor valve" and the steam bypass system are ineffective in this condition. Both are located downstream of the closed isolation valves and can no longer be reached by main steam.

Actions, in this order:
1. Initiate SCRAM (header, press twice). With the normal steam path unavailable, reactor power must be reduced. In the boiling water reactor, rising pressure additionally reduces the core void fraction and therefore introduces positive reactivity.
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems section). Under these conditions it provides the heat sink. The system is effective only if the reactor is shut down, main steam is isolated and sufficient inventory remains. Therefore complete step 1 first.
3. Monitor containment pressure. The safety valves discharge steam into the suppression chamber from 78 bar. If containment pressure exceeds 3.5 bar, open "Containment vent" (same section).

If "Main steam isolation stuck" is also active, the isolation valves cannot be reopened. The sequence above is then the available heat-removal path.
alarm_srv_open_help:
A safety valve has opened. It opens automatically at 78 bar dome pressure and closes again once pressure has decreased sufficiently. No direct operation of the safety valve is required.

The discharged steam does not reach the condenser but enters the suppression chamber inside containment. This increases the thermal and pressure load on containment. Prolonged discharge reduces the remaining pressure margin.

Actions — correct the cause of high pressure:
- If "MSIV closed" is active, the normal steam path is unavailable. Shut down the reactor and use "Isolation condenser" (see corresponding help text).
- Otherwise, open "Governor valve" (Secondary Circuit panel) further or reduce reactor power — in the boiling water reactor using "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel).
- Monitor containment pressure at the same time.
alarm_cont_press_high_help:
Containment pressure is above 3.5 bar. Steam discharged through the safety valves enters the suppression chamber and increases containment pressure. Above 4.3 bar, containment fails in the scenario.

Actions:
1. Set "Containment vent" to "open" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems section) before design pressure is reached. This allows pressure to be reduced in a controlled manner.
2. Correct the cause of the pressure increase so that no further steam is discharged into containment. Reduce reactor power and establish an appropriate heat sink (see "Dome pressure high").

With the reactor operating at high power, vent capacity is insufficient to compensate for a large continuing steam inflow. Following a reactor trip, heat input from decay heat is much lower. Therefore terminate reactor power first and then control containment pressure.

If a high hydrogen concentration is present at the same time, vent as early as possible. Additional hydrogen may accumulate as time passes.
alarm_h2_critical_help:
Hydrogen has accumulated from the simplified zirconium-water reaction. Restore cooling: the IC needs DC, and the diesel fire-water pump needs low reactor pressure and available water.

Controlled venting removes gas to the stack. High containment loading can independently cause leakage into the air-filled reactor building, where a flammable mixture may form. The game assumes ignition at the concentration threshold; venting alone does not trigger an explosion.
alarm_orm_low_help:
Indicated shutdown margin is below 30 equivalent rods. Do not withdraw further rods or force a power increase. If xenon causes the power controller to keep withdrawing rods, lower its setpoint or select manual control.

Act early: manual movement shares the graphite displacer effect of AZ-5 for highly withdrawn rods. The helper does not perform blind rod insertion.
alarm_orm_critical_help:
Indicated shutdown margin is below 15 equivalent rods. Avoid this operating condition.

In the historical RBMK, initially moving highly withdrawn rods can add positive reactivity. This applies to manual insertion as well as AZ-5; manual insertion does not bypass the graphite displacer effect. The helper therefore does not insert rods automatically in this condition.

Do not force a power increase or withdraw additional rods. Maintain coolant flow. The two-bank model only approximates spatial rod worth.
alarm_void_positive_help:
Increasing steam void fraction adds positive reactivity at this operating point. Maintain coolant flow and avoid further rod withdrawal or a forced power increase.

For highly withdrawn rods, manual insertion can also initially add positive reactivity. Monitor indicated shutdown margin together with the reactivity balance.
alarm_mcp_cavitation_help:
Subcooling is below 4 K while flow is above 90% of nominal. Pump inlet conditions are therefore close to saturation. Steam bubbles can form at the suction side and collapse again in regions of higher pressure. This can damage pump impellers and reduce delivered flow.

Actions:
1. Reduce "Main circulation pumps" (Primary Circuit panel). Lower flow reduces the pressure decrease at the pump suction and therefore reduces cavitation.
2. Check drum pressure. It should be close to 69 bar. If pressure is too low, saturation temperature falls and subcooling decreases.
3. Check drum level. Insufficient feedwater allows hotter, steam-containing water to return to the pumps.

Note for step 1: In the RBMK, lower coolant flow simultaneously increases the core steam void fraction and therefore adds positive reactivity. Reduce flow gradually and monitor reactor power.
alarm_graphite_hot_help:
Graphite temperature is above 760 °C. The moderator is therefore operating at an elevated temperature. Because of the long thermal time constant of approximately 35 minutes, graphite temperature responds slowly to power changes and also decreases slowly after power is reduced.

Actions:
- Reduce reactor power and maintain the lower level. A visible temperature response takes time; increasing power again after only a few minutes would therefore be premature.
- This alarm alone is not a reactor-trip criterion, but it indicates that the reactor has been operated at high thermal load for an extended period.
alarm_axial_tilt_help:
Axial power distribution differs by more than 35%. The upper or lower region of the core is therefore producing substantially more power than the opposite region.

The usual cause is a xenon oscillation rather than the control-rod position itself. In regions with higher neutron flux, xenon is depleted more strongly, changing local reactivity, while xenon poisoning increases in the opposite part of the core.

Actions:
- Do not increase reactor power until the axial power profile has become more uniform. Depending on the xenon condition, this can take several hours; the oscillation period is approximately half a day.
- Check "Control rods" (Reactor Core panel). In the RBMK, both groups move together, so their ability to correct an axial xenon distribution selectively is limited.
- See the fundamentals glossary, "Xenon poisoning (iodine pit)".
az5_hint: AZ-5 drives every rod in over 18 seconds — graphite tips first.
scn_free_desc: No orders, no score. The plant is yours.
scn_pwr_feedwater_loss_brief:
15 minutes at the pressurized water reactor with grid demand at 1400 MW. After three minutes, just one fault occurs: feedwater control switches to manual with its output set to zero. This is not a permanent pump failure. Automatic control can be restored; auxiliary feedwater is not modelled. Event advance warnings are enabled, and automatic fixes are permitted according to your settings.

Open the Secondary loop panel in advance and monitor Feedwater and steam generator level. At full power, indicated level can fall below 25% within seconds. The detailed briefing explains the controls. Alarm help and the fundamentals glossary remain available.

The run ends after 15 minutes unless fuel damage occurs or a trip-level alarm remains continuously active for more than 180 seconds without reactor shutdown. Acknowledging an alarm does not correct its cause. SCRAM is allowed; reaching the time limit does not validate a diagnosis or a particular sequence of actions. The debrief records the usual operating metrics.
scn_pwr_feedwater_loss_hint:
1. Check steam generator level and the Feedwater control mode in the Secondary loop panel. If control switches to manual with zero output, restore Feedwater to automatic immediately. Do not wait for an alarm.
2. If level is already below 25% or the corresponding trip-level alarm is active, initiate SCRAM (header, press twice), then restore automatic feedwater control. The alarm panel does not shut the reactor down for you.
3. Acknowledge alarms and check that feedwater flow resumes and SG level settles near 50%. Also monitor pressuriser pressure and level; decay heat still needs to be removed after SCRAM.
4. Do not rush to reset or reconnect the turbine. The shift can be completed with the reactor shut down.

Model limit: the fault only sets the controller to manual/zero. It does not prevent returning to automatic or changing manual output; there is no permanent pump damage or auxiliary feedwater system here.
scn_pwr_sg_tube_leak_title: Steam generator tube leak: independent assessment
scn_pwr_sg_tube_leak_brief:
15 minutes at the pressurized water reactor with a single, simplified steam generator tube leak. No event advance warning and no automatic fixes. Assess pressuriser level, SG level and feedwater flow together. Alarm help and the fundamentals glossary remain available.

This fault adds a constant 8 kg/s to the water mass of the lumped steam generator and lowers pressuriser level. It represents neither a complete primary leak mass balance nor a pressure-dependent leak rate. Individual steam generators cannot be isolated, and activity measurement is not available. Even SCRAM does not stop the leak. The chosen rate is limited for this short observation period, not for indefinite continued operation.

Completion only means reaching 15 minutes without fuel damage or a trip-level alarm remaining continuously active for more than 180 seconds without reactor shutdown. At this rate, doing nothing can also reach the time limit. There is no automatic diagnosis assessment; the normal operating metrics do not certify correct leak management.
scn_pwr_sg_tube_leak_hint:
A falling pressuriser level with approximately constant SG level does not rule out transfer into the secondary loop: feedwater control can compensate for the additional mass input. Compare trends rather than individual level readings. Pressure and level are not interchangeable in this simplified model.

Reducing reactor power lowers thermal loading but does not remove the imposed leak flow. After shutdown, cooldown can further reduce pressuriser level. A stable SG level therefore does not prove that the leak has been fixed. Individual SG isolation and activity measurement are unavailable; a complete real-world accident procedure is not represented here.
scn_pwr_combined_faults_brief:
18 minutes at the pressurized water reactor with several overlapping faults. There are no event advance warnings or automatic fixes. Assess the current plant condition independently; alarm help and the fundamentals glossary remain available.

Core cooling, heat removal and adequate water inventories take priority over grid demand. Existing plant controllers and the pressure-operated steam bypass continue to follow the model; this is not automatic fault repair. Trip-level alarms do not initiate SCRAM for you.

Model limit: loss of feedwater control means manual mode with zero output, not a permanent pump failure. Automatic control can still be restored; auxiliary feedwater is not modelled.

The shift ends after 18 minutes unless fuel damage occurs or a trip-level alarm remains continuously active for more than 90 seconds without reactor shutdown. Shutdown is allowed; acknowledgement alone is insufficient. There is no diagnosis test or prescribed sequence of actions as a completion criterion; elapsed time and the usual operating metrics are evaluated.
scn_pwr_combined_faults_hint:
Safety before electricity production: assess reactor power, heat removal and water inventories together. Reassess the whole plant after a change in conditions; an initial response may not have addressed every cause.

Take active protection alarms seriously, account for decay heat and do not force a restart. No advance warning, automatic fixes or detailed control sequence: set priorities from the indications.
scn_pwr_load_follow_brief:
Day shift at the pressurized water reactor. Around midday, grid demand decreases as numerous large consumers reduce their load at the same time. Your plant must follow the resulting demand curve: first reduce output in a controlled manner, then increase it again during the afternoon.

During normal operation, the automatic rod control system compensates for these load changes through small control rod movements. During the shift, however, one control rod group becomes stuck. From this point onward, further reactivity control must rely mostly on boration/dilution. Anticipating the required changes is essential: a change in boron concentration does not affect the reactor core until roughly three minutes later. If corrections are made only after a power deviation has already become visible, reactor output will continuously lag behind the demand curve.

What matters:
• Follow the demand curve — as long as the rod control system operates correctly, "Rod control" (Reactor core panel) handles this automatically.
• Once the rod group becomes stuck, use "Boric acid" (Reactor chemistry panel): dilution increases reactor power, while adding boron reduces it.
• Account for the three-minute delay: make small adjustments early, then select "Stop". Corrections made too late can cause the reactor power to overshoot.
scn_pwr_turbine_trip_brief:
Full-power operation at the pressurized water reactor. After ten minutes, a turbine trip occurs without warning. The generator is immediately disconnected from the grid. Unlike many real plants, this turbine trip does not by itself trigger an automatic reactor trip — the reactor keeps running at full power, and the resulting steam is routed directly to the condenser through the steam bypass system.

The sudden loss of turbine load simultaneously moves the pressurizer and steam generator water level away from their normal operating conditions. Once the plant begins to stabilize, a second fault occurs: the automatic feedwater control system fails. From this point onward, the steam generator water level must be controlled manually while the plant pressure gradually stabilizes.

Two individually manageable faults therefore occur in rapid succession.

What matters:
• Following the turbine trip, the steam bypass system opens automatically at 72 bar and directs steam to the condenser. No manual operation is required — concentrate on the pressurizer and steam generator water level.
• If feedwater control fails: switch "Feedwater" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and maintain the water level at approximately 50%.
• Only once the plant has stabilized should you select "Reconnect turbine" (Generator and grid panel) and then slowly increase "Load demand".
scn_bwr_flow_brief:
Three hours of load-following operation at the boiling water reactor. This time, reactor power is controlled not through the control rods but through recirculation flow — the standard method for smaller and faster power changes at this plant.

Grid demand decreases around midday and rises again during the afternoon. Power is adjusted by changing the coolant flow through the reactor core. Throughout the maneuver, the operating point must remain inside the permitted power-flow operating map.

Particular attention is required in the region combining high reactor power with low coolant flow. In this part of the operating map, power oscillations may develop whose amplitude no longer decays but instead continues to increase.

During the shift, recirculation pump output is reduced without warning. Coolant flow therefore decreases without any preceding operator action, moving the operating point closer to the critical region of the operating map.

What matters:
• "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) is the power-control variable in this scenario — increasing flow removes more steam voids from the core and increases reactor power within seconds, without moving the control rods.
• Rule of thumb: flow first, power second. Reversing that order can move the operating point through the restricted region of the operating map.
• If "Recirculation low" appears, coolant flow is already too low. Increase flow first — do not attempt to maintain reactor power using the control rods.
scn_bwr_msiv_brief:
Full-power operation at the boiling water reactor. The first few minutes pass without any abnormalities. After seven minutes, however, the main steam isolation valves close without warning.

The steam path to the condenser is now interrupted. Pressure inside the reactor pressure vessel rises rapidly. At the same time, the higher pressure reduces the steam void fraction inside the core. Fewer steam voids result in stronger moderation and therefore additional positive reactivity.

In a real plant, a full main steam isolation valve closure like this would automatically trigger a reactor trip within seconds. In the control room, that decision is yours — the protection systems warn, but you're the one who acts. Only a few seconds remain to carry out the required actions.

What matters:
• "Governor valve" and the steam bypass system are ineffective in this situation — both are located downstream of the closed isolation valves and can no longer be reached by the main steam flow.
1. Scram (header, press twice).
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section). The system is effective only when the reactor is shut down — therefore step 1 must be completed first.
3. Monitor containment pressure and, above 3.5 bar, select "Containment vent".
scn_rbmk_night_brief:
Night shift at the RBMK during a planned grid test. Reactor power is to be reduced from 1000 to 200 megawatts, held there for a defined period and then increased again.

At around 200 megawatts, however, a particular operating condition develops. Xenon concentration in the core increases and reduces the available reactivity. To maintain the specified power level, the control rods must be withdrawn further.

At the same time, the shutdown margin decreases — the number of equivalent control rods remaining in the core and available for a safe shutdown. Below 30 equivalent rods, the plant is already outside the permitted operating range. Below 15 equivalent rods, a particularly critical condition exists: when AZ-5 is initiated, the graphite tips of the inserting control rods can initially introduce additional positive reactivity before the actual shutdown effect becomes dominant.

During the shift, the power control system also fails. Shortly afterwards, two main circulation pumps fail. Both faults must be controlled manually while the shutdown margin may continue to decrease.

What matters:
• The shutdown margin (ORM) is the decisive parameter. Below 30, the plant is outside the permitted operating range; below 15, initiating AZ-5 can initially cause reactor power to increase.
• If "Power controller" (Reactor core panel) fails, control reactor power manually using "Control rods → Withdraw/Insert".
• If pumps fail: "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel). Lower coolant flow results in a higher steam void fraction and therefore POSITIVE reactivity — make adjustments slowly and continuously monitor reactor power.
• If necessary, reduce reactor power and insert control rods. Restoring an adequate shutdown margin takes priority over precisely following the demand curve.

Manual insertion can also initially add positive reactivity for highly withdrawn rods. Preserve margin early; manual motion does not bypass the graphite displacer effect.
scn_pwr_porv_brief:
Steady full-power operation at the pressurized water reactor. At some point during the first fifteen minutes, the pressurizer relief valve opens as intended to relieve a brief pressure increase. It then fails to close completely.

The dangerous aspect is that the control room continues to indicate the valve as shut. In reality, coolant is continuously escaping from the primary circuit. As a result, both pressurizer pressure and pressurizer water level decrease.

The alarm panel provides early indications of the developing fault. If only the indicated valve position is considered, however, the actual coolant loss may remain unnoticed. The subcooling margin decreases first, followed by a reduction in the safety margin against boiling at the fuel surface — the DNBR margin.

A comparable discrepancy between the indicated and actual valve position played a major role in the 1979 Three Mile Island accident.

What matters:
• The critical parameter is the subcooling margin — not the pressurizer water level alone. If it falls below zero, the coolant is no longer safely below its boiling temperature.
1. Set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel). This immediately stops the coolant loss.
2. Scram.
3. Set "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and increase heater power; close "Pressuriser spray" until pressure stabilizes.
• At Three Mile Island, step 1 was not carried out until approximately two and a half hours later.
scn_bwr_fukushima_brief:
The earthquake trips and isolates the reactor. The isolation condenser removes decay heat. The later tsunami interrupts AC and DC power; IC valves close and indications freeze.

In the game, replacement batteries can be connected under Safety systems. They allow the IC to operate again and the reactor depressurization valves to open. Battery deployment time is simplified.

The diesel fire-water pump only delivers below 12 bar and has a finite water supply. It needs no grid power. Depressurize the reactor first; this consumes vessel inventory and loads containment. Manage the IC and controlled containment venting. Venting is not an explosion switch: hydrogen can leak into the air-filled reactor building.
scn_bwr_instab_brief:
Full-power operation at the boiling water reactor with grid demand remaining high. The output of the main recirculation pumps drops noticeably over several minutes without operator input, and coolant flow through the core decreases with it.

Reactor power does not respond immediately. If the original power level is maintained by withdrawing control rods while recirculation flow remains low, the operating point shifts toward the critical region of the power-flow operating map: high reactor power combined with low coolant flow.

Density-wave oscillations can develop in this region, with their amplitude increasing progressively. Once the oscillations become sufficiently strong, the OPRM power limitation system is triggered.

No automatic reactor trip is initiated in this scenario. If this condition is reached, the reactor trip must be initiated manually.

What matters:
• Increasing "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) is the primary countermeasure: higher coolant flow directly damps the density-wave oscillation.
• If "Instability" appears, the condition can still be corrected by increasing coolant flow. If "Oscillation" (OPRM) appears, a scram must be initiated.
• The alarm panel indicates the condition but does not trigger an automatic shutdown. A scram must be triggered manually using the control in the header.
scn_rbmk_mcp_title: Loss of a Circulation Pump Group
scn_rbmk_mcp_brief:
Full-power operation at the RBMK-1000, with the power controller set to manual — as was standard practice for this reactor type historically, so you are managing reactivity from the very start. After ten minutes, two of the eight main circulation pumps trip without warning.

Coolant flow through the core decreases. Less flow means more steam voids in the coolant channels — and at this operating point, the RBMK's void coefficient is positive: more voids bring more reactivity, more reactivity brings more power, more power brings even more voids. Without correcting via the control rods, the process reinforces itself — nothing catches it automatically.

What matters:
• Reduce power promptly using the control rods. That is the actual countermeasure — running the remaining "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel) faster only partially makes up for the missing flow.
• Keep an eye on drum pressure and level while the plant settles into its new operating point.
• Left unattended, power will keep climbing until it trips "Power high".
scn_rbmk_cold_brief:
The plant is hot and pressurized but subcritical. All rods are inserted and main circulation pumps are stopped. This is a simplified hot restart, not a thermal cold start.

Start the pumps first. Grid demand remains zero for the first 30 minutes. Raise power carefully as demand increases. Monitor period and shutdown margin; target 900 MW and at least 30 indicated equivalent rods.

Historical RBMK: initially inserting highly withdrawn rods can add positive reactivity, including manual insertion. Avoid a low shutdown margin.
debrief_floor: Minimum score for a successful shift
fail_grid_deviation: Grid demand missed for too long
alarm_grid_deviation_warn_help:
Actual power differs significantly from grid demand ("Deviation" in the Grid panel). If this deviation remains continuously active for long enough, the shift is considered failed. This alarm is an advance warning and does not itself initiate a trip.

Actions:
1. Adjust core power to match grid demand. If demand is close to 0 MW, keep reactor power low even if the reactor is technically capable of producing more power.
2. When automatic control is active, check which parameter is actually being controlled. Some controllers maintain a pressure setpoint rather than directly controlling electrical load.
3. If the deviation cannot be reduced in time, a SCRAM resets the active timer. This carries a point penalty in the reactor-trip evaluation.
alarm_grid_deviation_trip_help:
The deviation between actual power and grid demand is still present and is approaching the permitted time limit. If it remains for a few more minutes, the shift is considered failed.

Actions:
1. Immediately reduce or adjust core power until it matches grid demand again.
2. If the deviation cannot be corrected sufficiently within the remaining time, initiate SCRAM. This immediately resets the timer but carries the corresponding point penalty.
debrief_rate_limited: too soon after the last one
save_slots_intro: Ten slots for this reactor type. Clicking a used slot overwrites it.
load_failed: Save does not match this reactor
btn_scram_resa_title: Reactor trip — all control rods insert
btn_scram_az5_title: Emergency protection, category 5 — all rods insert over 18 seconds, graphite tips first
login_rate_limited: Too many attempts. Please wait a minute.
login_expired: Your session expired. Please sign in again.
hint_gov: In manual you hold the valve position yourself — power follows.
hint_fw: In manual you fill or drain the steam generator yourself.
hint_pzr: Heating raises pressure, spray lowers it.
hint_rods: In manual you drive the rods with Withdraw and Insert.
hint_low_power: At very low power, thermal power barely tells you anything -- it stays at 0.0% long before anything is actually happening. Period and reactivity balance react much earlier and already show progress while you withdraw rods.
hint_annun: Click a tile to see what to do.
fail_trip_ignored: A trip condition stood without a shutdown
alarm_rod_stuck_help:
One control rod group no longer follows its setpoint because its drive is blocked. The setpoint can still be changed, but the actual rod position remains unchanged. This rod group also cannot be fully inserted during a reactor trip.

Actions:
- Do not issue further movement commands to the stuck rod group. Otherwise the setpoint will continue to diverge from the actual position, making the real rod position more difficult to assess.
- Control reactivity using the alternative control variable available for the reactor type:
   - Pressurized water reactor: "Boric acid" (Reactor Chemistry panel). Adding boron reduces power; dilution increases it. The response is delayed by approximately three minutes, so make early, small adjustments.
   - Boiling water reactor: "Recirculation flow" (Primary Circuit panel). Higher flow reduces the steam void fraction and increases power; lower flow reduces power. The response occurs within seconds.
   - RBMK: use the remaining functional control rod groups.
- Monitor shutdown margin. A stuck rod group is not available to provide its full shutdown contribution during a reactor trip.
alarm_mcp_stuck_help:
One or more main circulation pumps have failed due to a malfunction, not through operator action. The "on" button for these pumps is therefore locked (greyed out) — they cannot be restarted for the rest of the shift.

Actions:
- Adjust reactor power using the control rods to match the reduced coolant flow. Less flow means more steam voids in the coolant channels, and at this operating point the void coefficient is positive — without correcting via the rods, power keeps climbing on its own.
- Do not push the remaining "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel) beyond the flow that is now actually available; that only partially makes up for the loss anyway, the control rods are the real countermeasure.
- Keep watching drum pressure and level while the plant settles into its new operating point.
alarm_msiv_stuck_help:
The main steam isolation valves are closed and cannot be reopened because of an actuator fault. Setting "Main steam isolation" to "open" does not change the actual valve position. The steam path to the turbine and condenser therefore remains permanently interrupted and the normal heat-removal path is unavailable.

"Governor valve" and the steam bypass system are also ineffective in this condition. Both are located downstream of the closed main steam isolation valves.

Actions, in this order:
1. Initiate SCRAM (header, press twice). Without an available steam path, dome pressure will otherwise continue to increase; safety valves will open and discharge steam into the suppression chamber, increasing containment pressure.
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems section). Under these conditions it provides the heat sink. The system is effective only if the reactor is shut down, main steam is isolated and sufficient inventory remains. Therefore complete step 1 first.
3. Monitor containment pressure. If it rises above 3.5 bar, open "Containment vent" (same section) before 4.3 bar is reached.
alarm_porv_stuck_help:
The pressurizer relief valve has remained open even though pressure has already fallen below its intended opening range. The valve does not close automatically. As long as it remains open, the primary circuit continuously loses coolant. Pressurizer pressure and level therefore decrease. With further pressure loss, subcooling margin is lost and increasing amounts of steam can form in the primary circuit.

This fault condition played a decisive role in the Three Mile Island accident in 1979. The open valve remained unrecognized for an extended period.

Actions, in this order:
1. Set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary Circuit panel). It is installed in series upstream of the relief valve and immediately stops the coolant loss.
2. Initiate SCRAM if this has not already occurred.
3. Switch "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and increase heater power; close "Pressuriser spray" until pressure stabilizes.

The key indication is the subcooling margin. If it falls below zero, no subcooling reserve remains and heat removal from the core becomes increasingly critical.
event_fuel_dispersal_body: Fuel enthalpy exceeded 963 J/g. The fuel has dispersed and the plant is lost. This is how a fast power excursion ends: more reactivity than the feedbacks could remove in the time available.
event_clad_failure_body: Cladding temperature stayed above 1204 °C for more than three minutes. Beyond that point the zirconium-water reaction sustains itself, generating its own heat and hydrogen with it. The core is lost — with no power excursion at all, purely from lost cooling.
event_coolant_loss_body: Subcooling stayed below zero for more than five minutes: the core was no longer sitting in water but in steam. Steam absorbs heat, it does not carry it away. From the moment subcooling goes negative you have minutes — that was the indication that mattered.
event_cont_failure_loss_body: Containment exceeded its design pressure of 4.3 bar and ruptured. The last barrier between fission products and the environment is gone. Venting in time would have relieved the pressure — a controlled release instead of an uncontrolled break.
opt_helper: Automatic fault assistance ("Fix problem" button on every alert, with a log of what it did)
confirm_menu_text: This leaves the current shift. The last save is at most a minute old (autosave) -- any progress since then is lost.
alarm_fix_none: Nothing to do right now — the condition is already gone or needs no action.
alarm_fix_unfixable: Can't be fixed automatically — the explanation above says what to do by hand.
helper_action_porv_block_close: Block valve closed — stopped the leak at the relief valve.
helper_action_fire_inj_on: Diesel fire-water pump enabled; delivery requires pressure below 12 bar and available water.
helper_action_rods_insert: Control rods commanded to insert, to raise the shutdown margin.
helper_action_power_ctl_manual: Power controller switched to manual, so the rods stay where they were driven in by hand.
helper_action_mcp_set: Main circulation pumps throttled back to {v} %.
gauge_power_th_help:
**Normal range:** 0–100%. A trip occurs above 110%.

Thermal power indicates the heat currently generated in the reactor core. Changes in reactivity directly affect this value.

**Too low:**
1. Withdraw the control rods gradually (Reactor Core panel).
2. PWR: Boric acid → Dilute (Reactor Chemistry panel). The effect is delayed by approximately 3 minutes.
3. BWR/RBMK: increase recirculation flow. Higher coolant flow reduces the steam void fraction in the core and therefore increases power without control rod movement.

**Too high:**
1. Insert the control rods.
2. PWR: Boric acid → Borate.
3. BWR/RBMK: reduce recirculation flow. In the BWR, do not reduce it excessively because the operating point may enter the instability region — see "Recirculation low".
4. If power can no longer be reduced in time: initiate SCRAM/RESA/AZ-5 using the header control; press twice.
gauge_fuel_temp_help:
**Normal range:** up to 1400 °C. Warning above 1700 °C; critical condition above 1973 °C for PWR/BWR or the corresponding reactor-specific limit.

Fuel temperature is primarily determined by reactor power and available heat removal.

A low value is not a fault condition and requires no action. It simply indicates low thermal loading or low reactor power.

**Too high:**
1. Insert control rods to reduce reactor power.
2. Check heat removal: verify "Reactor coolant pumps"/"Recirculation flow" and ensure the required coolant flow is available.
3. If temperature remains excessive despite reduced power: initiate SCRAM/RESA/AZ-5.
gauge_reactivity_help:
**Normal range:** −200 to +200 pcm.

Reactivity indicates whether the chain reaction is currently increasing or decreasing. Positive reactivity causes reactor power to rise; negative reactivity causes it to fall.

**Too negative:**
1. Withdraw control rods gradually.
2. PWR: Boric acid → Dilute.
3. Slightly negative reactivity is not automatically critical. Xenon buildup after a load reduction, for example, can introduce additional negative reactivity. Correct it only when reactor power actually falls below the required level.

**Too positive:**
1. Insert control rods.
2. PWR: Boric acid → Borate.
3. If reactor period is below 10 s or thermal power is already above 110%, initiate SCRAM/RESA/AZ-5 immediately. Do not attempt to correct the condition solely through normal control actions.
gauge_prim_pressure_help:
### Pressurized Water Reactor

**Normal range:** 140–168 bar.

Primary pressure keeps the coolant in the liquid state and provides the required subcooling margin.

**Too low:**
1. If "Relief valve stuck open" is active, first set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary Circuit panel). This stops the coolant loss. Pressure cannot be stabilized permanently while the leak remains open.
2. Switch "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and increase heater power.
3. Close "Pressuriser spray" if it is open.

**Too high:**
1. Switch "Pressuriser spray" to manual and open it.
2. Reduce "Pressuriser heaters". Do not operate heating and spray against each other simultaneously.
3. Perform power changes more slowly. Rapid increases in reactor power are a common cause of high primary pressure.

### Boiling Water Reactor / RBMK

For the BWR and RBMK, this value corresponds to steam-generator, dome or drum pressure because there is no separate pressurizer.

**Normal range:** BWR 58–76 bar, RBMK 55–73 bar.

**Too low:**
1. Switch the control valve (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and close it further. Reduced steam removal increases pressure.
2. Reduce grid demand if the control valve is to remain in automatic mode.
3. Withdraw control rods gradually to increase steam generation.

**Too high:**
1. Switch the control valve to manual and open it further.
2. Insert control rods to reduce reactor power.
3. Above the respective pressure limits, the bypass system and then the safety valves open automatically. These systems limit pressure but do not replace timely control action.
gauge_subcooling_help:
**Normal range:** 15 K or higher. Below 8 K indicates increased risk. There is no problematic too high condition.

Subcooling margin indicates the temperature difference between the coolant and its boiling temperature at the current pressure. The smaller this difference becomes, the smaller the thermal margin to boiling.

**Too low:**
1. PWR: follow the actions under Primary Pressure → **Too low**. Increasing primary pressure increases the subcooling margin.
2. BWR/RBMK: increase primary, dome or drum pressure. Alternatively or additionally, reduce reactor power by inserting control rods so that less heat is transferred to the coolant.
3. RBMK additionally: check the main circulation pumps and ensure sufficient coolant flow. Low flow makes the condition more severe — see "Pump cavitation".
gauge_dnbr_help:
**Normal range:** 1.8 or higher. Below 1.3 indicates danger. A high value is not a problem.

DNBR or CPR represents the safety margin against a critical deterioration of heat transfer at the fuel rods. As the value decreases, the margin to the boiling limit becomes smaller.

**Too low:**
1. Insert control rods to reduce reactor power. This is the fastest normal control action.
2. Check "Reactor coolant pumps"/"Recirculation flow" and ensure the required pump operation and coolant flow.
3. PWR additionally: check primary pressure and subcooling. Low pressure may be the cause even if reactor power itself is not unusually high.
4. If these actions are insufficient: initiate SCRAM/RESA/AZ-5.
gauge_sg_press_help:
For the BWR and RBMK, this value is identical to the Primary Pressure gauge. See that section for the corresponding actions.

### Pressurized Water Reactor

**Normal range:** 55–76 bar. Secondary pressure is independent of primary pressure.

**Too low:**

Common causes are excessive steam removal or excessive/cold feedwater flow.

1. Reduce "Feedwater" (Secondary Circuit panel).
2. If excessive steam removal is the cause, check the control-valve position and grid demand.

**Too high:**
1. Switch "Governor valve" to manual and open it further.
2. Alternatively, reduce grid demand until pressure stabilizes.
3. The steam bypass system opens automatically at 72 bar and the safety valves at 88 bar. Both functions limit pressure but do not replace timely control using the control valve.
gauge_sg_level_help:
**Normal range:** 40–70%. Below 25% is dangerous; above 70% increases the risk of water being carried into the steam path.

The level must remain high enough to maintain sufficient heat transfer or core coverage, while remaining low enough to prevent water from entering the steam system.

**Too low:**
1. Switch "Feedwater" (Secondary Circuit panel) to manual and increase flow.
2. BWR additionally: if level decreases substantially, core coverage can be lost. If the value approaches the 25% trip threshold, do not unnecessarily delay RESA.
3. If AC power is no longer available: use "Diesel fire-water pump (below 12 bar)" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems). This system requires no motor or electronics but provides a significantly lower flow rate.

**Too high:**
1. Switch "Feedwater" to manual and reduce flow.
2. Check whether the elevated value is only a temporary automatic-control overshoot following a load change. In that case, the level may stabilize without additional intervention.
gauge_generator_help:
Generator power has no fixed too low or too high range. The relevant value is the deviation from current grid demand (Generator and Grid panel, "Deviation").

**Generator power below demand:**
1. Increase reactor power, for example by gradually withdrawing control rods. See Thermal Power.
2. Check the control valve or turbine controller. If the valve remains too far closed despite automatic operation, switch to manual and open it further.
3. If "Turbine tripped" is active, stabilize the plant first. Then use "Reconnect turbine". This is only possible when no reactor trip remains active. Afterwards, increase grid demand gradually.

**Generator power above demand:**
1. Reduce reactor power, for example by inserting control rods.
2. If necessary, reduce control-valve opening or turbine output.
gauge_cont_press_help:
Boiling water reactor only.

**Normal range:** up to 70% of the design limit. A low value is not a problem.

Containment pressure increases in particular when steam is discharged through the safety valves into the suppression chamber.

**Too high:**
1. Eliminate the cause of the continuing pressure increase: reduce reactor power or initiate SCRAM so that steam generation decreases substantially.
2. Set "Containment vent" to "open" (Secondary Circuit panel, Safety Systems). This is the active means of reducing containment pressure.
3. If hydrogen concentration is also high, vent as early as possible and monitor the further increase in pressure and hydrogen concentration.
